paras: The Rochelle shooting and lynching threats took place in Rochelle, Georgia, on a Saturday night in May 1888, when a Black man accused of shooting a Mr. Walker with a shotgun was jailed amid threats to lynch him. Walker suffered only a scalp wound, and no attempt on the jailed man was reported, though the Savannah Morning News wrote that "at one time lynching was feared."

According to the Savannah Morning News, Walker and his companion, a Mr. Harrold, both believed the shot had been meant for Harrold. The paper explained that Harrold and the accused man had been "engaged on opposite sides" in a riot at Eastman years earlier, and it suggested the man had sought to settle that old quarrel.

Shortly after dark, while Walker was walking with Harrold, a man the paper called "a negro man" shot Walker in the head with a shotgun. The shot entered the front of his head and glanced off the bone, leaving a scalp wound; he was given medical attention and the shot was soon found. The accused was arrested at once and placed in the county jail.

Once word spread that a man had been shot "in so cowardly a manner," there were, in the paper's words, "numerous threats of making short work of the would-be assassin." The report does not say who made the threats, and it describes no crowd at the jail or move against the prisoner.
The coverage does not name the accused man or report any trial or later outcome.

The only known report appeared on May 23, 1888, as a short paragraph in the Savannah Morning News's roundup of Georgia news, printed between items about a Confederate veterans' reunion and an Atlanta jail case. The item named Walker and Harrold but called the accused only "the negro" and "the would-be assassin," and it presented his motive as what "it is thought." It mentioned the lynching threats without comment, either approving or condemning them.
